Enums, Traits, and Generics

Enums and match

Enums with payload variants and exhaustive match work as a Rust programmer expects. Note the surface detail in the verified form: match arms take blocks, and a statement-level match is closed with a semicolon.

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

enum Status {
    Ready,
    Running,
    Failed(i32),
}

fn describe(status: Status) -> void {
    match status {
        Status::Ready => { println("ready"); },
        Status::Running => { println("running"); },
        Status::Failed(code) => { println("error {}", code); },
    };
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    describe(Status::Ready);
    describe(Status::Running);
    describe(Status::Failed(42));
    return 0;
}

Verified output: ready, running, error 42, exit code 0.

Traits and impl

Trait declarations, impl Trait for Type, and the &self receiver mirror Rust. Both call forms dispatch — the dot call and the fully qualified call:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

trait Score {
    fn score(&self) -> i32;
}

struct Item {
    value: i32,
}

impl Score for Item {
    fn score(&self) -> i32 {
        return self.value + 10;
    }
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let item = Item { value: 32 };
    println("{}", item.score());
    println("{}", Score::score(&item));
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 42, then 42 — item.score() and Score::score(&item) reach the same implementation. A second trait, over an f64 computation:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

trait Area {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
}

struct Circle {
    radius: f64,
}

impl Area for Circle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        return 3.14159 * self.radius * self.radius;
    }
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let c = Circle { radius: 5.0 };
    let a = c.area();
    println("{}", a);
    if a < 78.0 { return 1; };
    if a > 79.0 { return 2; };
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 78.5397500000, exit code 0.

Generic Functions with Built-In Bounds

A generic function bounded by a built-in trait is defined and called by bare name; the type argument is inferred from the arguments, as in Rust:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn max<T: PartialOrd>(a: T, b: T) -> T {
    if a > b {
        return a;
    } else {
        return b;
    }
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    println("{}", max(10, 20));
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 20, exit code 0. There is no turbofish: max::<i32>(10, 20)-style explicit type arguments are a parse error in SLA — inference is the only route, which is why the call forms matter below.

LimitationA generic free function bounded by a user-defined trait cannot be called yet. The definition below is accepted, but the call is rejected:
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

trait Score {
    fn score(&self) -> i32;
}

struct Item {
    value: i32,
}

impl Score for Item {
    fn score(&self) -> i32 {
        return self.value + 10;
    }
}

fn calculate<T: Score>(value: &T) -> i32 {
    return value.score();
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let item = Item { value: 32 };
    println("{}", calculate(&item));
    return 0;
}
Type Check Error: failed to verify types: Undefined call: calculate (error.UndefinedVariable)

Round-4 verification (2026-11-20) tried every plausible call form: bare name with a borrowed argument and with a by-value argument; dropping the bound; binding the argument to a concretely typed local first; binding the result with an explicit i32 annotation; and the trait-qualified form Score::calculate(&item), which is parsed as a trait-method lookup and rejected with a different diagnostic (Type Item does not implement trait method Score::calculate). All fail. Until this closes, the working patterns are the two verified above: bound a generic function on a built-in trait (PartialOrd), or skip the generic wrapper and call the trait method directly — by dot call or by qualified call, both of which dispatch today.

Key Points of This Page

  • Payload enums and match work as in Rust; statement-level match closes with a semicolon.
  • Trait methods dispatch by dot call and by qualified Trait::method(&x) call.
  • Generic functions bounded by built-in traits (e.g. PartialOrd) are called by bare name with inference; there is no turbofish syntax.
  • A generic free function bounded by a user-defined trait cannot be called yet (Undefined call) in any tested call form — call the trait method directly instead.
